★★★ THE arm64 GAS ASSEMBLY DIALECT — the SECOND assembly language, and the experiment that tests whether `asm.lang.json` is a shared core or a generalization of one dialect (plan 29 P2.6, 2026-08-13).

★★★ THE RESULT OF THAT EXPERIMENT, STATED FIRST BECAUSE IT IS THE WHOLE POINT: `asm.lang.json` NEEDED NO CHANGE. Its seven line-structure rules (`asmLine`, `asmElement`, `asmDirective`, `asmStatement`, `asmStatementTail`, `asmLabelTail`, `asmOperandSeq`) and its four standalone holes (`lineEnd`, `labelSeparator`, `directiveIntroducer`, `asmStandaloneOperand`, plus the two shared with the embedded surface) received this dialect unmodified — not one rule edited, not one hole added, not one `{optional}` widened. What this document writes is a token table, ONE operand production with five subordinate rules, and a vocabulary table. That is the reuse claim, MEASURED rather than asserted, and the governing anchor's own stated test ([[project_inline_asm_own_language_2026_08_12]]: *"the honest test of the core is whether it needs ANY change"*).
⚠ THE CLAIM IS SCOPED TO THE LINE GRAMMAR, WHICH IS WHAT `asm.lang.json` ACTUALLY OWNS. It is NOT a claim that the text→LIR ENGINE needed no change: it did, and those changes are findings in their own right (the sigil-less name resolution below, and the `operandForms` role taxonomy). Conflating 'the shared GRAMMAR held' with 'nothing had to change' is exactly the over-claim this project keeps having to walk back.

★★★ HOW FAR THIS DIALECT IS FROM AT&T, WHICH IS WHY IT IS A HONEST TEST AND NOT A COPY WITH RENAMED RULES. Every axis that a 'shared token table with knobs' design would have had to parameterise is different here, and one of them is not parameterisable at all:
  • REGISTER SIGIL — AT&T `%rax`, arm64 `x0`. There is NO sigil, which is not a smaller version of a sigil: it makes a register and a symbol LEXICALLY IDENTICAL (see `armName`).
  • IMMEDIATE SIGIL — AT&T `$42`, arm64 `#42`.
  • ★★ AND `#` IS AT&T's LINE COMMENT CHARACTER. This single byte is the measurement that made a dialect a LANGUAGE rather than a `.target.json` knob: in `asm-x86_64-att.lang.json` `#` opens a comment that runs to end-of-line; here it opens a VALUE. No token table can hold both, so the two dialects cannot share one — not 'awkwardly', but in principle.
  • LINE COMMENT — AT&T `#`, arm64 `//` (and `/* */`, which both share).
  • MEMORY OPERAND — AT&T `disp(base,index,scale)`, arm64 `[base, #off]`. Different opening token, different nesting, different position for the displacement.
  • OPERAND ORDER — AT&T `destinationLast` (`subq %rcx, %rax`), arm64 `destinationFirst` (`sub x0, x1, x2`). And arm64's three-operand form means the destination is not even one of the inputs, where AT&T's two-address form requires that it is.
  • MNEMONIC SPELLING — the two tables overlap by coincidence on `mov`/`add`/`sub`/`mul`/`ret` and diverge everywhere else: bitwise OR is `orr`, XOR is `eor`, NOT is `mvn`, shifts are `lsl`/`lsr`/`asr`, load/store are `ldr`/`str`, call is `bl`, branch is `b`.

★★ WHAT THIS DOCUMENT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT KNOW, exactly as its AT&T sibling does not: which registers exist, which opcodes exist, or how anything encodes. `x0` resolves through `TargetSchema::registerByName` and `mov` through `TargetSchema::opcodeByMnemonic`; an unresolvable name is a precise diagnostic naming the target. A register list in this file would be the target identity leak the bar forbids — and it would be a particularly tempting one here, because the sigil-less surface makes 'just declare the register names as tokens' look like the easy fix for `armName`'s ambiguity. It is the wrong fix and it is refused by name; see `armName`.

language.$comment:
★ THE NAME CARRIES BOTH AXES (`asm` · `arm64` · `gas`), the sibling convention. `gas` rather than `arm64-att`: the AArch64 assembly surface has no AT&T/Intel-style two-dialect split, so the ASSEMBLER is the axis that distinguishes it (a future `asm-arm64-armasm` for Arm's own tool is the sibling this shape leaves room for).
⚠ THIS DOCUMENT CLAIMS `.s`/`.S` TOO, AND THAT MAKES THE EXTENSION AMBIGUOUS ACROSS DIALECTS — the ambiguity is REAL rather than a bug in this file, and it is now DEMONSTRATED rather than predicted: with this document shipped, `.s` genuinely names two languages. An assembly file is target-specific BY NATURE (no `.s` compiles for both x86_64 and arm64), so 'which dialect' is answered by the TARGET, not by the extension. Until a driver reads that answer off the target, `--language asm-arm64-gas` names it explicitly, which is what the examples corpus does. Anchored: D-DRIVER-ASM-DIALECT-SELECTED-BY-TARGET (the row predates this file; this file is the second witness it was waiting for).
language.name: AsmArm64Gas

$isaComment: ★★★ THE ARCHITECTURE THIS LANGUAGE EMITS (D-ISA-LANGUAGE-BOUND-TO-ARCHITECTURE) — the AT&T twin carries the full argument; read that file's copy and keep the two in step. ★★ THE VALUE IS `aarch64`, MATCHING `arm64.target.json`'s DECLARED `isa` AND NOT THAT TARGET'S `name` (`arm64`) NOR THIS DOCUMENT'S OWN NAME (`asm-arm64-gas`). Both of those are IDENTITIES — the strings a user types — while this is the fact both sides declare about the hardware, and the gate compares only the declared values. That the three spellings differ is the measurement: a rule keyed on any name would have to invent a mapping table, and this one does not have a table at all.

languageReferences.$comment:
★★★ THE SHARED LINE STRUCTURE, REACHED BY REFERENCE — AND THIS BLOCK IS BYTE-FOR-BYTE THE SAME SHAPE AS THE AT&T DOCUMENT'S, WHICH IS THE MEASUREMENT. `entry: "asmLine"` imports exactly the rules reachable from it and NOTHING of the embedded `__asm__(…)` surface (the entry-closure scoping in `mergeLanguageReferences`), so this dialect owes the standalone holes plus the ones shared with the embedded surface — not every hole `asm.lang.json` declares.
★ THE BOUND TOKENS ARE THE SAME ROLES the AT&T document binds, to DIFFERENT kinds of this document's own. Same roles, different vocabularies, one grammar: the property the mechanism exists to have, now witnessed by a second signatory rather than argued for by one.

★★★ THE TEMPLATE PLACEHOLDER ROLES ARRIVED 2026-08-15 (D-ASM-DIALECT-DECLARES-NO-OPERAND-PLACEHOLDER) AND THIS DIALECT IS THE ONE THAT NEEDED THEM MOST. ✔MEASURED: AArch64 has no register-PINNING constraint letter (this target declares `r`, `w`, `m`, `i` and none of them names a specific register), so an `__asm__` OUTPUT on arm64 can only be written through a placeholder — which means that until these five bindings existed, EVERY aarch64 asm output was unspellable and sqlite's own `hwtime.h` arm (`mrs %0, cntvct_el0`) could not be written at all.
★★ AND THE BINDING SPLIT IS THE INTERESTING PART, BECAUSE IT IS NOT THE SAME AS THE AT&T DOCUMENT'S. TWO of the five roles bind to kinds this document mints ONLY in its `asm-template` lexer mode (`%` -> PlaceholderSigil and `%l` -> PlaceholderLabelSigil), while `templateOperandIndex` binds to the ORDINARY global `IntLiteral` and `symbolicNameOpen`/`symbolicNameClose` bind to the ORDINARY `BracketOpen`/`BracketClose` this dialect already declares globally for its memory form — `[sp, #-16]` and `%[out]` genuinely use the same byte here, and the AT&T document had to declare a bracket of its own because x86 gas has none. Two dialects, one role set, two different vocabularies AND two different declaration sites: the sharpest witness this mechanism has produced.
★ No FIRST-set collision follows from reusing the bracket: `armMemory` opens with `BracketOpen` and the placeholder opens with the placeholder sigil, so the two alt branches stay disjoint — and `detectAmbiguousAlternatives` re-runs over the MERGED rule set, so that is checked rather than asserted.

$tokensComment:
⚠ THIS BANNER SITS AT DOCUMENT LEVEL, NOT INSIDE `tokens`. A key in the `tokens` map is a LEXEME — arbitrary source text — so there is deliberately no `$`-documentation carve-out there and a `$comment` inside the map would declare a token spelled `$comment`. (✔MEASURED on the AT&T document the first time it was loaded: 'value must be an array of meaning objects'.)

★★★ THE NEWLINE IS NOT WHITESPACE — the single most load-bearing line in any assembly dialect, restated here because getting it wrong is silent. Assembly is line-oriented: there is no statement terminator, so the newline IS the terminator. Flag `\n` as `EmptySpace` and `ret` on one line swallows the next line's `mov` as an operand — a WRONG PARSE, not a parse error. `LineEnd` therefore carries NO flags.
★ `\r` STAYS `EmptySpace` so a CRLF file behaves exactly like an LF one.

★★★ `#` IS THE IMMEDIATE SIGIL HERE AND THE LINE COMMENT IN `asm-x86_64-att.lang.json`. THIS IS THE PROOF, and it is a single byte: `mov x0, #100` and `movq $100, %rax  # set it` both contain `#`, one opening a VALUE and one opening a COMMENT. A shared token table parameterised by a `commentPrefixes` knob and an `immediatePrefix` knob would have to give this byte two incompatible meanings AT THE SAME TIME for the two dialects it serves. It cannot, so the table cannot be shared, so a dialect is a LANGUAGE. Every other difference in this file is a difference of degree; this one is a difference of kind.

★★★ THE CONDITIONAL-BRANCH MNEMONICS USED TO BE DECLARED AS LEXEMES HERE, AND THE TWELVE ROWS ARE GONE — D-ASM-DIALECT-IDENTIFIER-CONTINUATION-NOT-CONFIGURABLE, closed 2026-08-13. `b.eq` is ONE mnemonic in gas, but `.` is this dialect's `directiveIntroducer`, so an undeclared `b.eq` tokenized as Identifier(`b`) + DirectiveDot + Identifier(`eq`) and `asmStatement` died at the dot. The workaround leaned on a real tokenizer property (the id-start path probes the declared-lexeme table and a lexeme LONGER than the identifier run wins, so the 4-byte `b.eq` beat the 1-byte run `b`) and it WORKED — its cost was that every dotted spelling appeared TWICE, here and in `instructions[]`, and the pair had to agree. ⇒ replaced by `identifierClass.extraContinue` below, which is gas's own rule and needs no per-spelling declaration at all; see that block's banner. The twelve `instructions[]` rows are unchanged, and they are now the ONLY place a conditional branch is spelled.
⚠ `b.cs`/`b.cc` ARE gas ALIASES of `b.hs`/`b.lo` and are declared as such — two spellings of one condition, the same shape `.globl`/`.global` already has. Per [[feedback_reference_compilers_are_the_spec]] an alias real gas accepts is not optional.

⚠ NO `!`, NO `@`, NO `%`, NO `;`, NO `=`, NO `+`: pre/post-index writeback (`[sp, #-16]!`), symbol-type sigils (`@function` / `%function`), gas's statement separator and `.set`-style assignment are all real AArch64 gas syntax this dialect does not model yet. They are UNDECLARED rather than half-declared, so they fail loud at the TOKENIZER with 'unexpected character' rather than parsing into something else. Anchored: D-ASM-ARM64-GAS-SURFACE-INCOMPLETE.
⚠ AND ONE CONSEQUENCE OF THE `directiveIntroducer` CHOICE THAT IS EASY TO MISS: a gas LOCAL label (`.L1:`) opens with the directive dot, so `asmElement` routes it to `asmDirective`. ⓘ UPDATED 2026-08-13 — `asm.lang.json`'s `asmDirective` grew an `{optional asmLabelTail}` slot, so `.L1:` now PARSES here too, from the SHARED grammar and with ZERO bytes changed in this document (✔MEASURED on this dialect: `A0008 unknown assembler directive '.L3'` where it used to be `P0001 expected 'LineEnd' — got ':'`). That the fix reached a second dialect for free is the same reuse property this file's banner claims for the line structure — and it is the first change the shared core has ever needed, which is stated rather than glossed: the core held for a second dialect's VOCABULARY and did not hold for a form both dialects share.
⚠ THE CONSUMER HALF IS NOT DONE: a directive node carrying a label tail is a LABEL DEFINITION, and the walker still sends it to the directive-vocabulary lookup, so `.L1:` is parseable and not yet definable. Anchored: D-ASM-DOT-PREFIXED-LOCAL-LABELS-UNPARSEABLE (grammar half done) and D-ASM-DOT-PREFIXED-LABEL-NOT-DEFINED-BY-CONSUMER. The corpus still uses plain identifiers (`Lwin`, `Lfail`), which gas accepts identically.

★★★ `%%` IS A TOKEN OF ITS OWN (P5 wave 2, 2026-08-14) — THE ESCAPED PERCENT, DECLARED HERE FOR THE SAME REASON AS IN THE AT&T SIBLING AND WITH A DIFFERENT NEIGHBOUR. An embedded `__asm__` TEMPLATE is not a `.s` line: `%0` is an OPERAND PLACEHOLDER there and a literal percent must be written `%%`. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-14 on THIS port too (`aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc` 13.3.0, source fed as base64): extended `"A%%0B"` emits `A%0B` — the `%0` that appears after unescaping is NOT re-read as operand 0. So an unescape-then-scan design would bind `%%0` to operand 0: a silent miscompile the reference compiler does not have.
★★ THE MECHANISM IS LEXEME **LENGTH**, NOT DECLARATION ORDER — ✔MEASURED in `tokenizer.cpp`'s `longestMatch`, which probes DOWN from the longest declared lexeme, so the 2-byte `%%` beats the 1-byte `%` regardless of row order (and `nlohmann::json` sorts object keys, so file order does not survive the parse at all).
⚠ AND THE COLLIDING NEIGHBOUR IS DIFFERENT HERE, WHICH IS WHY THIS IS NOT A COPY: `%` is the REGISTER sigil in the AT&T document and the TYPE sigil here (`.type main, %function`). The escape has to be declared per dialect because the byte it escapes means something different in each — the same one-byte argument that made a dialect a language, one level down.
⚠ NO SHAPE REFERENCES `PercentEscape` YET, which is the correct interim state: a `.s` containing `%%` fails LOUD at the parser, exactly as gas rejects it, so nothing is accepted that the reference assembler refuses while the template surface is still being built.
$identifierClassComment:
★★★ `.` CONTINUES AN IDENTIFIER HERE — gas's OWN rule, and the row that DELETED twelve token declarations (D-ASM-DIALECT-IDENTIFIER-CONTINUATION-NOT-CONFIGURABLE, closed 2026-08-13).
★★ WHAT WAS HERE BEFORE, AND WHY IT HAD TO GO. `b.eq` is ONE mnemonic in gas — you cannot write `b . eq` — but `.` is this dialect's `directiveIntroducer`, so with `b.eq` undeclared the tokenizer produced Identifier(`b`) + DirectiveDot + Identifier(`eq`) and `asmStatement` died at the dot. The workaround was to declare all TWELVE conditional-branch spellings as LEXEMES in the map above, so every one appeared TWICE — once there and once in `instructions[]` — with the two required to agree. Both mismatch directions failed loud, so nothing was silent; the DUPLICATION was the defect, and it scaled with the vocabulary (`cbz`, `tbnz`, `b.al`, `b.vs`… each would have paid it again).
★★ THE FIX IS THE REFERENCE ASSEMBLER'S ACTUAL RULE RATHER THAN A SPECIAL CASE FOR `b.`: a gas symbol may CONTAIN a dot. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-13 — `aarch64-linux-gnu-as` assembles `foo.bar:` as a label and `.quad DW.ref.foo` as a symbol reference, both rc=0. So `b.eq`, `foo.bar` and `DW.ref.__gxx_personality_v0` all lex as ONE Identifier from ONE declaration, and `instructions[]` matches on the text exactly as before.
★★★ AND IT DOES NOT COLLIDE WITH THE OTHER TWO `.`-INITIAL CONSTRUCTS, BECAUSE IT ANSWERS A DIFFERENT QUESTION. `extraContinue` says what may appear INSIDE a name that has already started; it says nothing about what may START one, and `.` deliberately cannot (the facet has no `extraStart` key, and asking for one is refused by name at load). So a LEADING `.` is still the `directiveIntroducer` TOKEN, and `.L3:` versus `.text` versus `.section .rodata` are still separated exactly where they were — by `asmDirective`'s `{optional asmLabelTail}` slot and by the directive vocabulary. ⇒ ONE mechanism per question, not three that fight: leading dot ⇒ introducer token; interior dot ⇒ this key.

lexerModes.$comment: The two comment bodies, verbatim in shape from the AT&T dialect (which took them verbatim from `c-subset.lang.json`): every character inside becomes an `EmptySpace` CommentChar, and an unterminated body is reported as a comment rather than as a wall of stray tokens. The `endsAtExclusive` on `//` above is what keeps the terminating `LineEnd` OUTSIDE the comment body — without it a comment-terminated line loses its terminator and merges with the next.
lexerModes.$templateComment:
★★★ `asm-template` — THE SECOND LEXICAL SURFACE OF THIS DIALECT, AND THE SIBLING OF THE AT&T DOCUMENT'S MODE OF THE SAME NAME. ⚠⚠ IT IS EMPTY ON PURPOSE (inline-asm P5c, 2026-08-17 — D-SEMANTIC-ASM-TEMPLATE-SIGILS-HARDCODED-BESIDE-A-CONFIG-OWNER, CLOSED). It used to declare three rows — `%%`, `%`, `%l` — while `scanInlineAsmTemplate` compared against the same bytes as C++ literals: two owners of one fact, and nothing able to detect them disagreeing, because the semantic tier has no dialect in scope when it scans. The rows are now SYNTHESIZED by the loader from `asm.lang.json`'s `semantics.inlineAsmTemplateLexemes` (the LANGUAGE's bytes) joined to this document's `bindTokens` (this dialect's kinds) by ROLE NAME; declaring a template lexeme here is now a LOAD ERROR naming both sites. Not a body mode: no `defaultToken`, so the scanner runs its ordinary lexeme match and consults the synthesized table FIRST with the global table as fallback. Entered only by the TEMPLATE PARSE ENTRY, which reads the name from `assembly.templateLexerMode`; a `.s` never enters it.

★★ WHAT EACH SYNTHESIZED ROW BUYS HERE, AND THE THIRD IS THE ONE THAT NEEDS DEFENDING.
  • `templatePlaceholder` -> `PlaceholderSigil` (`%`) — the operand placeholder. `%` is `TypeSigil` globally here (`.type main, %function`), a DIFFERENT collision from the AT&T document's `RegisterSigil`, which is exactly why the KIND is still per dialect even though the BYTE no longer is: the byte being escaped means something different in each. The same one-byte argument that made a dialect a language, one level down — and it survives the change intact, because what moved is the byte, not the kind.
  • `templateLabelPlaceholder` -> `PlaceholderLabelSigil` (`%l`) — `asm goto`'s label sigil, two bytes so maximal munch settles `%l[done]` against `%0`. ⚠ It cannot shadow `lsl`/`ldr`/`ldp`: the lexeme starts at the percent.
⚠⚠ THE `%l` ROW IS THE GRAMMAR HALF ONLY — NOTHING LOWERS A LABEL PLACEHOLDER. It makes `%l[done]` LEX and PARSE; the lowering then refuses it by name, because a label target must resolve to a BLOCK of the function that embedded the template and an operand binding carries a register and no block. See `asm.lang.json`'s `asmTemplateLabelRef` for the full statement.
  • `templateEscape` -> `PercentEscape` (`%%`) — bound with **NO SHAPE REFERENCING THE KIND IN THIS DIALECT**, and that is deliberate rather than an oversight. AArch64 gas has no register sigil (`x0`, not `%x0`), so there is no `%%<reg>` form to accept — the AT&T document has one and this one does not. What the row buys is the MUNCH GUARD, a correctness property and not a convenience: ✔MEASURED 2026-08-14 on `aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc` 13.3.0 with the source fed as base64, extended `"A%%0B"` emits `A%0B` and the `%0` that appears is NOT re-read as operand 0. Without the row `%%0` would lex as PlaceholderSigil + PlaceholderSigil + IntLiteral and a placeholder scanner would find a lone `%` in front of the digit. With it the two bytes are consumed together and `%%0` reaches no shape at all — refused loud, which is what the reference toolchain does one stage later when gas sees the emitted `%0`. ⓘ It is also the one role no shared SHAPE spells; see `asm.lang.json`'s `$templateEscapeHoleComment` for why binding it is still legal.
  • `symbolicNameOpen`/`symbolicNameClose` -> `BracketOpen`/`BracketClose` (`[`/`]`) — ⚠ THESE TWO ROWS ARE NEW IN THIS MODE AND CHANGE NOTHING, which is stated rather than glossed. `[`/`]` are already GLOBAL in this dialect (the memory form), so before P5c `%[out]` reached them through the mode's global fallback; the synthesis now writes them into the mode as well. ✔MEASURED that the synthesized rows are byte-identical to the global ones — same kinds, `opensScope: Bracket` and `closesScope: true` — so the override and the fallback resolve to the same meaning and no input reads differently. The AT&T sibling, which has NO bracket of its own, genuinely needs the rows.
★★ THE ORDERING MECHANISM IS LEXEME **LENGTH**, NOT DECLARATION ORDER — ✔MEASURED in `tokenizer.cpp`'s `longestMatchInMode`, which probes DOWN from the longest key; `nlohmann::json` sorts object keys anyway, so a `.json` file's row order does not survive the parse. ⇒ a 'red on reordering' pin cannot exist. The pin that CAN exist now nulls the ROLE in `asm.lang.json` and watches this dialect's row disappear with it — stronger than the old row-deletion pin, which only proved two copies happened to agree.

numberStyle.$comment: gas integer literals: decimal, `0x` hex, `0b` binary and a leading `0` octal — the same set the AT&T dialect declares, because it is a property of GAS rather than of the CPU, and that is a real (small) piece of evidence about where the dialect boundary falls. No float literals: a floating-point CONSTANT in a `.s` appears only inside a `.double`/`.float` directive, which this dialect does not model (an undeclared directive fails loud). Declaring float syntax that cannot be lowered would be the accept-and-ignore this project refuses.

shapes.$comment: ★ ONLY THE ROOT AND THE OPERAND PRODUCTION LIVE HERE — six rules, and five of them are the operand. Everything between root and operand (the line, the label chain, the directive, the statement, the operand sequence) arrives from `asm.lang.json`. THAT SIZE IS THE MEASUREMENT: a second dialect's `shapes` block is the size of an operand grammar, not the size of an assembly grammar.

root.$comment:
An arm64 `.s` translation unit: a run of lines, each terminated.
★★ THE FINAL NEWLINE IS MANDATORY, for the reason the AT&T document measured and which is a property of the SHARED grammar rather than of either dialect: a trailing `{optional asmElement}` to accept an unterminated last line is refused by the loader as `C_AmbiguousAlternatives` — after any complete line an Identifier could open either another `asmLine` or the unterminated final element, and LL(1) cannot tell them apart. Making the terminator optional inside `asmLine` would remove the ambiguity by removing the LINE DISCIPLINE; `speculative: true` would put backtracking into the one grammar in this tree that has none; appending a newline would be the driver rewriting the user's source.
⇒ A file whose last line lacks a newline is a LOUD parse error at that line. That this reproduces identically in a second dialect is the evidence it is a shared-grammar property and not an AT&T quirk. Anchored: D-ASM-FINAL-NEWLINE-REQUIRED.

armOperand.$comment:
★★ ONE arm64 OPERAND — three FIRST-disjoint forms, no speculation:
  • `#100` / `#-8`   immediate → ImmediateSigil
  • `[x1, #16]`      memory    → BracketOpen
  • `%function`      symbol-type marker → TypeSigil
  • `x0` / `helper`  a NAME    → Identifier
★★★ AND THE LAST ARM IS THE FINDING THIS DIALECT EXISTS TO PRODUCE. AT&T needs FIVE arms because its sigils separate the forms lexically; arm64 needs three because it has almost no sigils — and the one it drops entirely, the REGISTER sigil, is the one that was doing the separating. `x0` (a register) and `helper` (a call target) and `Lwin` (a branch target) are THE SAME TOKEN. No grammar can split them, so `armName` is one rule serving three operand ROLES, and the split has to happen where the information actually lives: the TARGET's register table. See `armName`.

armSectionName.$comment:
★★★ `.rodata` IN OPERAND POSITION — the shape `.section .rodata` needed and no `armOperand` arm had (D-ASM-SECTION-DIRECTIVE-WITH-OPERAND-UNMODELLED, closed 2026-08-13). ✔MEASURED 2026-08-13 with BOTH reference assemblers: `.section .rodata` assembles rc=0 and produces a `.rodata` PROGBITS+A section, while a bare `.rodata` is `Error: unknown pseudo-op`. So the read-only data section is reachable ONLY through an operand, and until this rule existed the line died at the tokenizer/grammar seam with `expected 'LineEnd' — got '.'`.
★★ THE DOT IS MANDATORY AND IS NOT DECORATION. ✔MEASURED: gas's `.section rodata` (undotted) creates a section literally NAMED `rodata` with NO allocation flag — a DIFFERENT section from `.rodata`. Accepting the undotted spelling as a synonym would place data somewhere the reference assembler does not, so this rule requires the introducer and the consumer checks that the leading token IS this dialect's introducer (read off the tree, never hardcoded as `.`).
★ IT IS NOT BOUND TO AN `operandForms` ROLE, exactly like `armTypeMarker` beside it and for the same reason: a role is what an INSTRUCTION operand is lowered through, and this one is read as TEXT by the directive handler and resolved against this dialect's own section-opening directive ROWS. An unroled rule reaching instruction position fails loud in `decodeOperand` — the correct answer for `add x0, .rodata, x1`.
★ FIRST-DISJOINT WITH EVERY SIBLING ARM: `DirectiveDot` against `ImmediateSigil` / `BracketOpen` / `TypeSigil` / `Identifier|IntLiteral|MinusSign`. And disjoint from `asmLabelTail`'s `LabelColon`, so `asmDirective`'s two consecutive `{optional}` slots stay LL(1) with this arm in the operand set.

armTypeMarker.$comment:
★★ `%function` — THE SYMBOL-TYPE MARKER, AND A THIRD INDEPENDENT AXIS ON WHICH THE TWO DIALECTS DIFFER. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-13 in WSL: `aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc -S` emits `.type main, %function` while x86_64 `gcc -S` emits `.type main, @function`. Same directive, same meaning, different sigil — because `@` is a COMMENT character on 32-bit ARM and the ARM gas port never reclaimed it. ⓘ AArch64 gas ACCEPTS `@function` too (✔MEASURED, assembles rc=0), so this is a case where the dialects overlap and the reference COMPILER's choice is the one worth matching; only `%function` is declared, and an `@function` operand fails loud at the tokenizer rather than being silently accepted, which keeps 'what this dialect reads' honest.
★ IT IS NOT BOUND TO AN `operandForms` ROLE, deliberately: a role is what an INSTRUCTION operand is lowered through, and this one is read as TEXT by the directive handler and compared against the row's declared `marker`. An unroled rule reaching instruction position fails loud in `decodeOperand` — the correct answer for `add x0, %function, x1`.
★★ AND THIS IS THE SINGLE CLEANEST REFUTATION OF THE 'ONE TOKEN TABLE WITH KNOBS' DESIGN, because it is the SECOND byte to change meaning across the pair: `%` is the REGISTER sigil in `asm-x86_64-att.lang.json` (`%rax`) and the TYPE sigil here. Together with `#` (comment there, immediate here) that is two of the two sigil bytes inverted — not a knob setting, a different language.

armName.$comment:
★★★ A BARE NAME — A REGISTER *OR* A SYMBOL, AND THE GRAMMAR CANNOT TELL WHICH. `mov x0, x1`, `bl helper` and `b Lwin` all put a plain Identifier in operand position, because arm64 gas has no register sigil. This is not a gap in this file; it is the surface gas defines.
★★ THE RESOLUTION IS A TARGET LOOKUP, WHICH IS WHAT GAS ITSELF DOES: a name that `TargetSchema::registerByName` resolves IS a register; one it does not IS a symbol. That keeps the decision in the vocabulary tier where it belongs, costs this document no register list, and matches the reference assembler's own shadowing rule (a symbol named `x0` loses to the register — ✔ gas behaves this way, and per [[feedback_reference_compilers_are_the_spec]] matching it is the requirement, not a choice).
★★ HOW THIS DOCUMENT *DECLARES* THE AMBIGUITY, with no new config key: `operandForms` binds BOTH `register` AND `displaced` to THIS rule. Two roles on one rule is not a duplicate — it is the statement 'these two roles are lexically indistinguishable here, resolve them against the target', and it is exactly the fact an engine keyed on rule-identity alone needs to be told. A dialect WITH a sigil (AT&T) binds them to two different rules and gets the strict behaviour it should: `%foo` that names no register is an ERROR there, because the sigil already promised a register.
⛔ THE FIX THAT MUST NOT BE TAKEN, recorded because it is the obvious one and it looks clean: declaring `x0`…`x30`, `w0`…`w30`, `sp`, `xzr`, `d0`…`d31`, `v0`…`v31` as TOKENS in the map above. It would work, it needs no engine change, and it would put a 130-entry copy of the target's register file into a language document — the precise target identity leak the bar forbids, and the second copy would start drifting the day the target gained a register. Refused by name.

★★★ WIDENED 2026-08-13 FROM `sequence:[Identifier]` TO ALSO ACCEPT A BARE NUMBER — D-ASM-ARM64-BARE-SCALAR-OPERAND-UNPARSEABLE, and the trigger was the data directives below. `.quad 58` puts an `IntLiteral` in operand position, and this alt had NO arm for one, so it died at the parser with `expected 'LineEnd' — got '58'` — while `asm.lang.json`'s OWN `asmDirective` comment asserts that '`.byte 1, 2` (integers)' parses. The shared core was describing a capability one of its two dialects did not have.
★★ IT IS ALSO WHAT gas ACCEPTS, WHICH IS THE ACTUAL REQUIREMENT rather than a convenience: ✔MEASURED 2026-08-13, `aarch64-linux-gnu-as` assembles `mov x0, 5` and `add x1, x0, 3` rc=0 and encodes them as `#0x5`/`#0x3` — the `#` is OPTIONAL on this port. A dialect refusing a bare immediate was rejecting valid AArch64 gas in the instruction stream too, not only in data.
★★★ AND IT NEEDED NO NEW ROLE, NO NEW BINDING AND NO ENGINE CHANGE, which is the part worth checking against the bar. The existing `register`+`displaced` pair on this rule already resolves by TARGET LOOKUP, and that lookup answers the new case correctly for free: `registerByName("58")` fails exactly as `registerByName("helper")` does, so a number lands on `displaced` — which `assembly_config.hpp` defines as 'a scalar, optionally followed by a base'. That is precisely what AT&T's `attDisplaced` (`attScalar` + optional memory) already meant, so the two dialects now agree on the shape rather than one having a private hole. `decodeScalar` then reads it with the same token-join it uses for every other scalar, and `armNegNumber` under this alt keeps `.quad -1` signed through the SAME descent that fixed D-ASM-NEGATIVE-SCALAR-LOSES-ITS-SIGN.
⚠ ONE CONSEQUENCE ACCEPTED KNOWINGLY: `armMemory` uses this rule for its BASE, so `[58]` now PARSES. It does not assemble — `decodeMemory` refuses a base that names no register, loudly — and gas rejects it too, so the refusal moves from the parser to the consumer without becoming silent. Splitting a strict `armMemBase` off would buy a marginally earlier diagnostic and a second rule to keep in sync.

armImmediate.$comment: `#` + a scalar — `#100`, `#-8`, `#0x1f`, `#some_symbol`. gas also accepts a constant EXPRESSION here (`#(1<<3)`); this dialect models a single scalar and fails loud on anything else rather than accepting an expression it would then have to fold with semantics nobody declared. The AT&T dialect draws the same line at `$`, which is (small) evidence that where a dialect stops is a property of the shared design rather than of either CPU.

armScalar.$comment: The value inside an immediate: a number, a negated number, or a symbol name.

armNegNumber.$comment: `-8` — the ordinary negative displacement, as in `[x29, #-8]`. A separate rule (rather than a signed literal in `numberStyle`) because the sign is GRAMMAR: `-` is also a binary operator in gas expressions, and a signed-literal token would make `8-4` lex as two numbers.

armMemory.$comment:
★★ `[base]` / `[base, #off]` — AND THIS IS THE OTHER AXIS A SHARED TOKEN TABLE COULD NOT HAVE PARAMETERISED. AT&T writes the displacement OUTSIDE and the base inside parens (`-8(%rbp)`); arm64 writes both inside brackets with the displacement SECOND (`[x29, #-8]`). Different opening token, different nesting, different ORDER — three independent facts, not one knob.
★ The comma inside the brackets can never be confused with the operand-list separator: the choice at this position is between `OperandComma` (an offset follows) and `BracketClose` (the operand ends), which are distinct kinds, and the operand list's own `{repeat}` only resumes after this rule completes. Same argument the AT&T `attMemory` makes about its parens, which is a sign the shape is right rather than a coincidence.
⚠ NO INDEX-REGISTER FORM (`[x0, x1, lsl #3]`) AND NO WRITEBACK (`[sp, #-16]!`): both are real gas and both are UNDECLARED, so they fail loud rather than parsing into something smaller than what was written. Anchored under D-ASM-ARM64-GAS-SURFACE-INCOMPLETE.

armMemOffset.$comment: `, #off` inside a memory operand. Named rather than inlined so the consumer answers 'was there a displacement?' by RuleId — the same node-evidence discipline the shared grammar's fused section arms are built on.

pipelineEntry.$comment:
★★★ A `.s` TRANSLATION UNIT ENTERS AT THE ASSEMBLER'S INPUT. `encode` is the fourth tier (operator decision, plan 29 §5) and means post-regalloc, post-two-address-legalize, post-calling-convention. ✔MEASURED in `src/program/compile_pipeline.cpp`: a `.s` must enter after THREE passes and not one — `allocateRegisters` would reassign the programmer's registers, `legalizeTwoAddress` would rewrite the instruction forms, and `materializeCallingConvention` would inject a prologue/epilogue OVER the one the programmer wrote. Entering at `lir` silently reframes every hand-written function.
★ AND THERE IS NO `optimize: false` SIBLING: entering at `encode` means no MIR module exists, so MIR passes cannot run BY CONSTRUCTION. 'Hand-written assembly is not optimized' is a consequence of the tier, never a second switch that could drift from it.
★ THE ROW IS DECLARED HERE, IN THE DIALECT, NOT IN `asm.lang.json` — and that placement is load-bearing rather than tidy. A `byRule` row is matched by RULE NAME and every language's root is named `root`, so a `{"rule": "root"}` row in the shared core would resolve against a HOST language's translation unit and route every C file straight to the assembler, past HIR, MIR and the optimizer: a silent miscompile of an entire host language produced by a config that never mentions C.

assembly.$comment:
★★★ THE TEXT→LIR CONTRACT: the rule landmarks the lowering reads, the ONE dialect-wide operand-order fact, and the spelling vocabulary. Everything here is a NAME the engine resolves — no behaviour, no branch.

★★★ `operandOrder` IS `destinationFirst`, AND IT IS THE CLEANEST SINGLE-FACT CONFIRMATION THAT PUTTING IT AT DIALECT SCOPE WAS RIGHT. The reverted `asmSyntax` facet declared a destination flag PER INSTRUCTION on the theory that stores differ; ✔MEASURED false for AT&T, and measured false again here — arm64 is uniformly destination-FIRST including `str x0, [x1, #16]`, where the register written to MEMORY is still written first. Two dialects, both internally uniform, opposite values: exactly one fact, exactly one place to state it.
★★ AND THE TWO DIALECTS DIFFER IN A SECOND WAY THIS KEY DOES *NOT* HAVE TO CAPTURE, WHICH IS THE POINT OF DERIVING RATHER THAN DECLARING. AT&T's `subq %rcx, %rax` is TWO-ADDRESS (`rax = rax - rcx`); arm64's `sub x0, x1, x2` is THREE-ADDRESS (`x0 = x1 - x2`) and the destination is not an input at all. Neither document says so: `.target.json` already states `requires2Address` per opcode (true on x86_64's `sub`, absent on arm64's), and the lowering derives the operand mapping from that plus `result` plus this one order flag. A per-dialect two-address knob would have been a second source of truth for something the target already owns, and the two would have drifted.

★ `instructions[]` maps an ASSEMBLY SPELLING to TARGET OPCODE NAMES plus the operand WIDTH. ✔MEASURED and this is why the table exists at all: `opcodes[].mnemonic` is NOT assembly — the 80 arm64 entries are DSS's virtual-ISA names (`shr_l`, `jcc`, `store_outgoing_arg`, `lea_extern_got`), while a real `.s` writes `lsr`/`b.eq`/`str`/`adrp`. Several overlap by coincidence (`mov`, `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `ret`, `cmp`, `neg`, `sdiv`, `udiv`, `msub`), which is exactly what would have made reusing them LOOK like it worked — and the coincidence is WIDER here than on x86_64, so the trap is worse: `and` is a real arm64 mnemonic AND a real DSS opcode name, while `orr`/`eor`/`mvn`/`lsl`/`lsr`/`asr`/`ldr`/`str`/`bl`/`b` are all real arm64 mnemonics whose DSS names are something else entirely. A table that happened to be right for ten rows and wrong for ten more is the failure mode this mapping prevents.

★★ `opcodes` IS AN ARRAY, AND arm64's ROWS ARE MOSTLY SINGLETONS — WHICH IS EVIDENCE, NOT A WASTED FACILITY. The array exists because AT&T overloads ONE spelling across THREE DSS opcodes: `movq` is `mov` (`movq %rcx, %rax`), `load` (`movq (%rdi), %rax`) and `store` (`movq %rax, (%rdi)`), elected by the target's own `encoding.variants[].guard.operandKinds`. arm64 does NOT overload: `mov`, `ldr` and `str` are three spellings, so three rows of one opcode each. ⇒ the overloading is a DIALECT property, which is a second independent argument for the array living in the dialect document rather than in the target.

⚠ `width` IS DECLARED 64 ON EVERY ROW, AND THAT IS AN HONEST DEFAULT RATHER THAN A COMPLETE ANSWER. On AT&T the width is in the MNEMONIC SUFFIX (`movq`→64, `movl`→32), so a per-spelling constant is exactly right. On arm64 the width is in the REGISTER NAME — `add x0, x1, x2` is 64-bit and `add w0, w1, w2` is 32-bit with the SAME mnemonic — so a per-spelling constant cannot express the 32-bit form, and every row here therefore describes the x-register form only. ⇒ the moment `w0`…`w30` exist in the target, a `w`-register operand must either DRIVE the width or FAIL LOUD; silently encoding a 64-bit ADD for `add w0, w1, w2` would be a miscompile with no diagnostic. Anchored: D-ASM-DIALECT-WIDTH-SOURCE-IS-DIALECT-DEPENDENT.
assembly.$templateSurfaceComment:
★★★ THE THREE KEYS THAT MAKE AN EMBEDDED `__asm__` TEMPLATE READABLE BY THIS DIALECT (2026-08-15, D-ASM-DIALECT-DECLARES-NO-OPERAND-PLACEHOLDER; third key added P20). OPTIONAL AS A SET, REQUIRED OF EACH OTHER — the loader refuses any proper subset, because a mode with no rule mints placeholder tokens no shape accepts, a rule with no mode declares a shape whose FIRST token nothing ever produces, and a surface with no LABEL rule cannot tell an `asm goto` target from an operand; all three are silent no-ops.
★ `templateLabelRule` names the LABEL alternative of the placeholder rule, which is how the engine asks `resolveBranchTarget` rather than `resolveRegister` without ever testing the `%l` bytes in C++.
⚠⚠ THE SET IS MANDATORY FOR THIS DOCUMENT RATHER THAN OPTIONAL — a consequence of `D-CONFIG-ASM-TEMPLATE-CAPABILITY-NO-LONGER-OPTIONAL-FOR-A-SHARED-SURFACE-IMPORTER`, not a new policy: `asm.lang.json`'s `asmLine` closure SPELLS the template holes. The argument lives once, in `assembly_config.hpp`'s `templateLabelRule` docblock.
★ ON THIS TARGET THE SET IS WHAT MAKES AN ASM OUTPUT POSSIBLE AT ALL — `arm64.target.json` declares the constraint letters `r`/`w`/`m`/`i` and none of them PINS a register, so an output has nowhere to be captured from except the placeholder's own vreg. That is not a gap in the target description: AArch64 genuinely has no register-pinning constraint letter, which is why gcc's own `hwtime.h` writes `mrs %0, cntvct_el0` here and `"=a"`/`"=d"` on x86.
assembly.$spellingCaseComment:
★★★ gas IS CASE-INSENSITIVE ON EVERY SPELLING IT DECLARES, AND DSS WAS NOT — D-ASM-DIALECT-MNEMONIC-MATCH-IS-CASE-SENSITIVE. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-15, `aarch64-linux-gnu-as` (GNU Binutils for Ubuntu) 2.42, rc plus the encoded word read back with `aarch64-linux-gnu-objdump -d`: `mov x0,x1` / `MOV X0,X1` / `MoV x0,X1` all encode `aa0103e0`; `mov w0,w1` and `MOV W0,W1` both encode `2a0103e0`; `add x0,x1,x2` and `ADD X0,X1,X2` both `8b020020`; and the two SELECTOR-carrying spellings this dialect declares fold too — `mrs x0, cntvct_el0` and `MRS X0, CNTVCT_EL0` both `d53be040`, `cset x0, eq` and `CSET X0, EQ` both `9a9f17e0`. Directives likewise: `.TEXT`, `.GLOBL`, `.TYPE`, `.SECTION`, `.DATA`, `.XWORD` all rc=0. Refusing what the reference assembler accepts is a defect under [[feedback_reference_compilers_are_the_spec]], so this dialect folds — and it folds ALL FOUR surfaces (mnemonic, register, operand selector, directive) or none: a fold that stopped at the mnemonic would still refuse `MOV X0, X1` at the register, which hides the gap instead of closing it.

★★ THE SELECTOR HALF IS WHY THE KEY IS ON THE DIALECT AND NOT ON THE TARGET. `cntvct_el0` and `eq` are spellings THIS dialect declares in `instructions[].operandSelectors`; `x0` is a spelling the TARGET declares. One key folds both because both are DECLARED VOCABULARY being matched against written text — and `TargetSchema::registerByName` still compares exactly, so nothing about `arm64.target.json` changes and a future dialect for this same CPU may choose the other policy.

⛔ WHAT THIS KEY DOES **NOT** REACH, MEASURED IN THE SAME RUN: (1) SYMBOL/LABEL names — `foo:` and `FOO:` are two defined symbols in one object and `b FOO` against `foo:` leaves `FOO` `*UND*`; (2) the `.type` MARKER — `.type main, %FUNCTION` and `%Function` are BOTH rc=1 *"unrecognized symbol type"* while `.TYPE` itself is accepted; (3) the `.section` NAME operand — `.section .RODATA` opens a section literally called `.RODATA`. Folding any of the three would merge two things gas keeps apart, which is a miscompile and not a conformance fix.

operandForms.$comment:
Which of THIS document's rules realizes each operand ROLE the lowering understands. The engine walks ROLES, never rule names — which is what let a dialect whose memory form is `[base, #off]` reuse the lowering unchanged, exactly as the AT&T document predicted it would.
★★★ TWO ROLES SHARE ONE RULE, AND THAT SHARING IS A DECLARATION RATHER THAN AN ACCIDENT: `register` and `displaced` both name `armName`, which states 'a bare name is either a register or a symbol and only the target can say which'. See `armName` for why no grammar can split them and why declaring the register file here is refused.
⚠ `indirect` ALSO NAMES `armName`, AND THAT ONE IS A CONTRACT ARTEFACT WORTH NAMING. arm64 has NO indirect-operand marker at all: AT&T writes `jmp *%rax` and puts the indirectness in the OPERAND, arm64 writes `br x0` and puts it in the MNEMONIC (`b` vs `br`, two `instructions[]` rows mapping to `jmp` and `jmp_indirect`). So the honest declaration is 'this dialect has no such form' — but `operandForms` REQUIRES all seven roles, correctly, so that a partial block cannot silently mean 'this operand shape is unrecognized'. It is therefore declared `null` — an EXPLICIT absent, which the loader distinguishes from an omission (an omitted role is still a load error, so a partial block can never silently mean 'this operand shape is unrecognized'). ★ ALIASING IT ONTO `armName` WAS THE FIRST ATTEMPT AND IT WAS WRONG TWICE OVER, which is why the wrong version is recorded here rather than just deleted: it put THREE roles on one rule, tripping the undecidable-pair check (`displaced` and `indirect` are both non-register, so no target lookup can separate them), and it asserted a form this dialect does not have. The role set really was AT&T's operand taxonomy generalized once — that finding was real; the fix was an absent-declaration in the shared loader rather than a per-dialect workaround. Closed: D-ASM-DIALECT-ABSENT-OPERAND-ROLE.

instructions.$comment: ★ DATA MOVEMENT. `mov` is the one spelling whose two target variants (`["reg"]` and `["imm32"]`) are variants of the SAME opcode, so the row is a singleton and the target's own guard elects between `mov x0, x1` and `mov x0, #100` — no dialect involvement, which is the division of labour this table is supposed to have. ★★ NO `width` KEY, AND ITS ABSENCE IS LOAD-BEARING (D-ASM-ARM64-GAS-MOV-ROW-PINS-WIDTH-64, 2026-08-13). This row USED to declare `width: 64`, and `effectiveWidth` reconciles a row-declared width against the width DERIVED from the register operands — so `mov w0, w1` was REFUSED outright ("the spelling and the registers disagree"). That is the whole point of the aarch64 model: the REGISTER SPELLING carries the width here, unlike AT&T x86 where the mnemonic SUFFIX does (`movl` vs `movq`) — D-ASM-DIALECT-WIDTH-SOURCE-IS-DIALECT-DEPENDENT. ⚠ THE FINDING THAT MATTERS: the target's W-form ORR variant was added the PREVIOUS cycle specifically so a hand-written `.s` could write `mov w0, w1` — and a `.s` could not write it, because of this key. Neither half was wrong on its own; they were never connected. Every row below whose target opcode declares BOTH an explicit width:32 and an explicit width:64 variant has had the key dropped for the same reason; the rows that KEEP it are the ones whose target opcode has only width-ABSENT variants, where dropping it would let a W-register spelling silently elect a 64-bit word.

★ ARITHMETIC — THREE-ADDRESS, unlike AT&T's two-address forms. Nothing here says so: `.target.json` omits `requires2Address` on these opcodes and the lowering derives the shape. `add x0, x1, x2` therefore produces result=x0, operands=[x1, x2], where `addq %rcx, %rax` produces result=rax, operands=[rax, rcx].

★ BITWISE — AND THE CLEAREST STRETCH OF THE TABLE WHERE THE SPELLINGS AND THE DSS OPCODE NAMES DIVERGE. gas writes `orr`/`eor`/`mvn`; DSS's virtual ISA calls them `or`/`xor`/`not`. Only `and` coincides, which is precisely the coincidence that makes reusing opcode mnemonics as spellings look workable until it silently is not.
★★★ THE `width: 64` PINS ARE GONE FROM `and`/`orr`/`eor` — D-ASM-ARM64-BITWISE-W-FORMS-UNDECLARED, closed 2026-08-13, and the ROW ABOVE IS NOW TRUE OF ALL FOUR SPELLINGS RATHER THAN ONE. The pins existed because the target declared `and`/`or`/`xor` with a SINGLE width-ABSENT variant each, and a width-absent variant matches ANY width — so dropping a pin before the target grew its W-form would have let `and w0, w1, w2` elect the 64-bit word. The target now declares AND/ORR/EOR at BOTH widths (0x0A000000 / 0x2A000000 / 0x4A000000 beside 0x8A000000 / 0xAA000000 / 0xCA000000, every one ✔MEASURED against `aarch64-linux-gnu-as` 2.42), so the width comes from the REGISTER SPELLING exactly as `mvn`/`lsl`/`lsr`/`asr` already take it — D-ASM-DIALECT-WIDTH-SOURCE-IS-DIALECT-DEPENDENT, and the same reasoning that removed the `mov` row's pin.
⚠ WHAT THE PIN WAS ACTUALLY COSTING, stated because it is NOT what the anchor's title says: with `width: 64` declared, `effectiveWidth` reconciled the row against the register-derived width and REFUSED `and w0, w1, w2` outright ("the spelling and the registers disagree") — a fail-loud, not a miscompile. The silent half of this defect was never in the dialect at all; it was in the C path, where a 32-bit `int` AND elected the width-absent X-form and emitted a 64-bit instruction. Removing these three pins is what lets a `.s` write the W-form; declaring the target variants is what fixed the C path.

★ CONTROL FLOW. `b` is the unconditional branch (DSS `jmp`), `br` the register-indirect one (DSS `jmp_indirect`) — the indirectness is in the MNEMONIC here, where AT&T puts it in the operand (`jmp *%rax`). `bl` is the call and `ret` the return.

★★ THE CONDITIONAL BRANCHES — one row per condition, each naming a `TargetCondCode` that ALREADY EXISTS. No new vocabulary was minted for this dialect: `eq`/`ne`/`slt`/`sle`/`sgt`/`sge`/`ult`/`ule`/`ugt`/`uge` are the same names `.target.json`'s `condCodeEncoding` maps to AArch64's 4-bit cond field, and the same ones the C front-end's comparisons already produce. ⚠ THE SIGNED/UNSIGNED PAIRING IS THE PART TO GET RIGHT AND IS EASY TO GET WRONG: gas's `lt/le/gt/ge` are SIGNED, and its unsigned peers are spelled `lo/ls/hi/hs` (with `cc`/`cs` as accepted aliases of `lo`/`hs`) rather than with a `u` prefix — so a table built by pattern-matching the letters would map `b.ls` to `sle` and miscompile every unsigned comparison silently.
⚠ THIS BLOCK USED TO END BY NAMING `cset x0, eq` AS DELIBERATELY ABSENT — 'it needs a condition-code operand ROLE the grammar has no form for'. ✅ THAT IS NO LONGER TRUE: the twelve `cset` rows below declare the condition as a POSITIONAL OPERAND SELECTOR, which needed no new role and no grammar form (D-ASM-ARM64-CONDITION-AS-OPERAND-UNMODELLED, closed 2026-08-14). The diagnosis in the old sentence was right — `eq` really does arrive as a bare Identifier that would decode as a register-or-symbol — and the remedy it assumed (a new operand role) was the wrong one: the operand is not an operand at all, it is part of the mnemonic.

★★★ `cset <Xd>, <cc>` — THE CONDITION AS A POSITIONAL OPERAND SELECTOR, and the close of D-ASM-ARM64-CONDITION-AS-OPERAND-UNMODELLED (operator ruling, plan 29 §4.7, 2026-08-14). The row directly above this block used to say this spelling was DELIBERATELY ABSENT because `eq` 'would arrive as a bare Identifier and decode as a register-or-symbol'. That was true and is now fixed at the seam where it was actually broken: `operandSelectors` says operand 1 is part of the MNEMONIC, so it is consumed by the match and the lowering sees exactly one operand — `x0`, the destination — against `setcc`'s `maxOperands: 0`. No new operand ROLE, no condition-code grammar form, no engine branch.
★★★ TWELVE ROWS MIRRORING `b.eq`…`b.cs` EXACTLY, AND THE PAIRING IS THE PART THAT IS EASY TO GET WRONG. gas's `lt/le/gt/ge` are SIGNED and its unsigned peers are spelled `lo/ls/hi/hs` (with `cc`/`cs` as accepted aliases of `lo`/`hs`) rather than with a `u` prefix — so a table built by pattern-matching the letters would map `ls` to `sle` and silently miscompile every unsigned comparison. ⚠⚠ `name` BESIDE `cond` IS THEREFORE **NOT ONE FACT WRITTEN TWICE**: `name` is the gas SPELLING and `cond` is the substrate's `TargetCondCode`, and DERIVING one from the other is precisely that letter-matching. Do not 'simplify' it.
★★★ ✔MEASURED 2026-08-14, `aarch64-linux-gnu-as` 2.42, one word per condition — and every one of the twelve is pinned against these bytes in `tests/asm/test_asm_shipped_dialects.cpp` rather than against a rule I believed: eq 9a9f17e0 · ne 9a9f07e0 · lt 9a9fa7e0 · le 9a9fc7e0 · gt 9a9fd7e0 · ge 9a9fb7e0 · lo 9a9f27e0 · ls 9a9f87e0 · hi 9a9f97e0 · hs 9a9f37e0 · cc 9a9f27e0 · cs 9a9f37e0. ⓘ `cc`/`cs` produce bytes IDENTICAL to `lo`/`hs`, which is what an alias means and is why both spellings are declared rather than one.
★★ THE INVERSION IS THE TARGET'S AND NOT THIS TABLE'S. `CSET Xd,cond` IS `CSINC Xd,XZR,XZR,invert(cond)`, and `arm64.target.json`'s `setcc` variant already declares `condInvert: true` at `condBitPos: 12` over fixedWord 0x9A9F07E0. So `cond: "eq"` (encoding 0) becomes nibble 1 in the wire word — ✔MEASURED to agree with gas on all twelve. A dialect that pre-inverted would double-invert and produce the complement of every condition, silently.
⚠⚠ THESE ROWS DECLARE **NO** `width`, AND UNTIL 2026-08-15 THEY DECLARED `width: 64` — READ WHY BEFORE PUTTING IT BACK. The old pin was NOT the `nop` row's reasoning; it was the `and`/`orr`/`eor` reasoning, and it was correct FOR AS LONG AS THE TARGET DECLARED ONE width-ABSENT `setcc` VARIANT. ✔MEASURED: gas accepts `cset w0, eq` and encodes 1a9f17e0, a genuinely different instruction from `cset x0, eq` (9a9f17e0) — and a width-absent variant matches ANY width, so a bare row would have derived 32 from the `w` register, elected the ONE 64-bit variant anyway and emitted the 64-bit word. That is a silent miscompile, so the pin shipped and the LOUD refusal it produced was anchored as D-ASM-ARM64-SETCC-W-FORM-UNDECLARED. ✅ THE ANCHOR IS CLOSED: `arm64.target.json` now declares `setcc` at width 64 (0x9A9F07E0) **and** width 32 (0x1A9F07E0), so dropping the pin makes each register spelling ELECT ITS OWN VARIANT instead of misencoding. ⛔ RE-ADDING `width` HERE WOULD RE-BREAK THE W-FORM — `effectiveWidth` would reconcile the declared 64 against the register-derived 32 and refuse `cset w0, eq`, a line gas takes. ⛔ AND DELETING EITHER TARGET VARIANT WOULD RE-OPEN THE MISCOMPILE THE PIN EXISTED FOR; the two edits are one edit, in both directions.

★ COMPARISON — sets the condition flags a `b.<cc>` then reads. `result: none` in the target, so the lowering must treat BOTH written operands as inputs rather than reading the first one as a destination; that is derivable from `result` and needs no dialect declaration.

★★★ `nop` — THE ZERO-OPERAND SPELLING, AND THE SECOND WITNESS FOR IT. `arm64.target.json` has declared this opcode (fixed word 0xD503201F, ✔MEASURED against `aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc` + objdump) with NO producer in any source language: `opcodeByMnemonic` resolved it, its encoder was pinned, and nothing could emit it. The AT&T sibling grows the same row in the same cycle, so the zero-operand path is exercised by BOTH dialects rather than by one — a mechanism witnessed by one signatory is the weaker claim this project keeps having to walk back.
★★ IT IS ALSO THE ONLY NON-TERMINATOR ZERO-OPERAND INSTRUCTION EITHER DIALECT CAN NOW WRITE. `asmStatement` mints NO tail child for a bare mnemonic, and until this row existed the shipped dialects reached that arm through `ret` alone — a terminator, which takes a different route through the lowering. ⚠ `ret` also hid the case in the ONE direction that matters here: a bare `nop` in the middle of a block must lower to an ordinary instruction and NOT close the block.
★ `width: 64` FOLLOWS THE `ret` ROW ABOVE. On this dialect a declared width is normally the thing to avoid — the REGISTER SPELLING carries the width here (D-ASM-DIALECT-WIDTH-SOURCE-IS-DIALECT-DEPENDENT), which is why the `mov`/`and`/`orr`/`eor` rows dropped theirs — but that reasoning is about reconciling a declared width against REGISTER operands, and this spelling has none. The target's single encoding variant is width-ABSENT (`guard.operandKinds: []`) and matches any width, so the key can never disagree with an operand that is not there.
⚠ THIS ROW USED TO END BY NAMING `cntvct` AS DELIBERATELY ABSENT — ✅ NO LONGER TRUE, see the `mrs` row below (D-ASM-ARM64-SYSTEM-REGISTER-AS-OPERAND-UNMODELLED, closed 2026-08-14). The old text's DIAGNOSIS was exactly right and is worth keeping: a plain `{"spelling": "mrs", "opcodes": ["cntvct"]}` row would take `mrs x0, cntvct_el0`, read `x0` as the destination per `destinationFirst`, and hand the lowering ONE leftover operand against `maxOperands: 0` — so EVERY line using it would fail loud, which is the read-as-support/deliver-an-error defect the `.cfi_personality` family is kept out of the AT&T table for. What was wrong was the assumed REMEDY (an operand ROLE the grammar has no form for). The operand is not an operand.

★★★ `mrs <Xd>, cntvct_el0` — THE HARDWARE COUNTER READ, and the close of D-ASM-ARM64-SYSTEM-REGISTER-AS-OPERAND-UNMODELLED (operator ruling, plan 29 §4.7, 2026-08-14). `arm64.target.json` declares `cntvct` (0xD53BE040) as AArch64's answer to RDTSC — the instruction sqlite's own `hwtime.h` reaches for on this CPU — and until this row existed the opcode had NO producer in any source language.
★★★ WHY THIS IS A SELECTOR AND NOT A SYSREG OPERAND KIND, WHICH IS THE WHOLE ARGUMENT. ✔MEASURED on BOTH shipped targets: x86_64 `rdtsc` is `min/maxOperands 0` with `implicitRegisters.outputs [rax,rdx]`; arm64 `cntvct` is `min/maxOperands 0` with `result: value` and the counter in the fixed word. They differ in RESULT MODEL — real, and fine — but BOTH are zero-operand with WHICH COUNTER baked into the opcode. ⇒ 'read the hardware counter' is ONE VERB across ISAs, and `cntvct_el0` is an AArch64 SPELLING detail exactly as `edx:eax` is an x86 one. Modelling it as a generic `mrs` + a sysreg operand would give the arm64 read a DIFFERENT SHAPE from the x86 read, so every shared consumer — starting with `hwtime.h`'s own lowering — would acquire a per-arch shape distinction: the `if (arch == …)` the bar hard-vetoes, arriving through CONFIG rather than C++, which is the slower and worse way for it to arrive. The target opcode's own $comment already made this argument ('a generic `mrs` could only ever read one system register') and it is the reason this row is spelled `mrs` while naming `cntvct`.
★★ THE SELECTOR IS CONSUMED BY THE MATCH: operand 1 never becomes an operand, never reaches the target, and is EXCLUDED from the `destinationFirst` reading — so the lowering sees exactly one operand (`x0`, the destination) and ZERO remaining, satisfying `maxOperands: 0` with nothing left over. ⚠ `index` IS DECLARED RATHER THAN ASSUMED BECAUSE THE MIRROR IMAGE PUTS IT FIRST: ✔MEASURED, gas writes `msr tpidr_el0, x0` (d51bd040) — selector at index 0 — and with `destinationFirst` a position-blind key would read the SELECTOR as the destination. NO `msr` ROW SHIPS (nothing needs one, and §A.2 cuts both ways); the point is only that the KEY is not wrong about it.
⚠⚠ `width: 64` IS REQUIRED, AND §4.7.2(3) PREDICTED IT WOULD NOT BE — the prediction is REFUTED by measurement, which is why that section says not to trust it. The premise holds: `cntvct`'s single encoding variant IS `guard.operandKinds: []`, i.e. width-absent. The INFERENCE does not, because a width-absent variant matches ANY derived width and this dialect derives width from the REGISTER SPELLING. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-14, `aarch64-linux-gnu-as` 2.42: `mrs w0, cntvct_el0` is REJECTED ('operand mismatch') — MRS always writes an X register. Without the pin, `mrs w0, cntvct_el0` would derive width 32, elect the width-absent variant and emit d53be040 anyway: accepting what the reference assembler rejects, which the bar forbids in both directions. With it, `effectiveWidth` reconciles and refuses loudly. This is the `nop` row's situation only in its premise; the conclusion is the opposite because `nop` has no register operand to disagree with.
★ ✔MEASURED 2026-08-14 with `aarch64-linux-gnu-as` 2.42 and pinned in `tests/asm/test_asm_shipped_dialects.cpp`: `mrs x0, cntvct_el0` → d53be040 — and `mrs x0, tpidr_el0` is a REAL system register gas assembles happily (d53bd040) that this dialect must refuse BY NAME rather than lower as if the operand had not been written. That refusal is what proves the selector SELECTS.
★ SELECTORS FORECLOSE NOTHING. If a target ever needs a sysreg carried as DATA into a real encoding slot, a generic operand kind COEXISTS with this row — the selector row is a SPECIALIZATION, the same relation `nop` has to a generic form — provided the loader's ambiguity refusal stays in place. Anchored trigger-gated: D-ASM-SYSTEM-REGISTER-AS-ENCODED-DATA-UNMODELLED.

directives.$comment: ★ A DIRECTIVE IS A VERB, NOT A STRING. The engine switches on the closed `verb` set; the SPELLING is this dialect's. gas's `.globl`/`.global` are two spellings of one verb — and that both dialects need exactly that pair is a small confirmation the verb/spelling split is at the right seam. An undeclared directive fails loud naming the spelling and this dialect, never ignored, because a silently-dropped `.globl` produces a binary whose entry symbol is local and a link failure that points nowhere near the cause.

⚠ BOTH SPELLINGS, AND ON THIS TARGET IT IS `.global` THAT THE REFERENCE COMPILER ACTUALLY EMITS — ✔MEASURED 2026-08-13, `aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc -S` writes `.global main` where x86_64 `gcc -S` writes `.globl main`, and AArch64 gas accepts either (assembles rc=0 both ways). A dialect that declared only the x86 habit would have failed on every aarch64 compiler output while looking complete.

★★★ `.type NAME, %function` — WHICH LABELS ARE FUNCTIONS, STATED BY THE FILE INSTEAD OF GUESSED BY THE COMPILER. Every label NOT so marked is a BLOCK inside whatever function is open, which is what makes `b Lwin` a branch rather than a call into a second function. The operator's ruling on the corpus: *"an example that only works because the compiler guesses is the example being wrong."*
★ `marker` IS WHY `.type foo, %object` DOES NOT MINT A FUNCTION — both are `.type`, and only the operand distinguishes them. That this row differs from its x86_64 sibling in exactly ONE string (`%function` vs `@function`) is the evidence the marker belongs to the dialect and not to the engine.

★★ THE DATA SECTIONS. `.data` and `.bss` are gas directives in their own right and keep their own rows.
★★★ `.rodata` IS NOT, AND THAT ASYMMETRY IS THE WHOLE OF D-ASM-SECTION-DIRECTIVE-WITH-OPERAND-UNMODELLED (closed 2026-08-13). ✔MEASURED 2026-08-13 against BOTH ports — `aarch64-linux-gnu-as` and x86_64 `as` — a bare `.rodata` is `Error: unknown pseudo-op` while `.section .rodata` assembles rc=0 into a `.rodata` PROGBITS+A section. Declaring `.rodata` as an ordinary row would make this dialect accept a spelling NO reference assembler does, which the bar forbids in both directions; leaving it out made read-only data unreachable. ⇒ the row below declares `operandOnly`, so the spelling exists in the SECTION vocabulary and not in the DIRECTIVE vocabulary, and writing it bare fails loud naming the form that works.
★★ WHAT THAT BUYS BEYOND `.rodata`, AND WHY IT MINTS NO SECOND TABLE: `.section` DELEGATES to these very rows, so `.section .data` and `.data` reach the identical row by construction (both ✔MEASURED accepted by gas) and `.section .text` reaches the `sectionText` row. A private section-name table hung off the `.section` row would have restated `.data`→data and `.bss`→bss — the same declared-twice shape the identifier-continuation facet just deleted twelve instances of — and the two copies would drift the first time a section was renamed.

★★★ `.section NAME` — THE SECTION IS THE OPERAND. It models the section NAME and NOTHING ELSE, and the boundary is stated rather than discovered: real `.section` also carries flags and a type (✔MEASURED, gas accepts `.section .rodata,"a",@progbits` and `.section .note.GNU-stack,"",@progbits` rc=0), every one of which changes what the section IS — `"aw"` writable, `"ax"` executable, `@nobits` zero-fill. DSS derives all of those from the `DataSectionKind`, so honouring the name while dropping the flags would put `.section .rodata,"aw"` in a read-only section the program then faults writing. ⇒ a `.section` with more than one operand FAILS LOUD naming the operand it will not interpret. Accept-and-ignore is the one thing not on the table.
⚠ CONSEQUENCE, STATED SO IT IS NOT REPORTED AS A SURPRISE: the `.section .note.GNU-stack,"",@progbits` line that ends nearly every gcc `-S` output is REFUSED — twice over, since `.note.GNU-stack` is also not a section this build can place.
⚠⚠ AND THE REFUSAL COMES FROM TWO DIFFERENT SITES, WHICH THE SENTENCE ABOVE USED TO ELIDE. 'Both refusals name what they refused' was true of the SECTION NAME and NOT of the flags spelling, and the difference is measurable. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-13 through the real CLI on THIS dialect: `.section .rodata,1` and `.section .rodata,%progbits` reach the directive handler and get `A0008 — '.section' carries 2 operands; this build models the section NAME and nothing else`, quoting the operand and stating the rule. `.section .rodata,@progbits` does NOT — `@` is a token in the AT&T sibling (it writes `.type main, @function`) and is not one here (this document writes `%function`), so it dies at `P000E: got illegal character 0x40`; the quoted form dies the same way at `0x22` on BOTH dialects, since neither declares a string literal. Every form refuses (rc=1, no artifact, the flags are never applied and never ignored) — there is no silent path — but only the lexable forms carry the explanatory message. Pinned from both ends in `tests/asm/test_asm_shipped_dialects.cpp`.
★ THE READ-ONLY DATA SECTION, reachable ONLY as `.section .rodata`. `operandOnly` is what keeps the bare spelling refused — see the `.data` row's banner for the measurement.

★★★ THE ELEMENT WIDTHS ARE THIS DIALECT'S, AND `.word` IS THE REASON THAT MATTERS. On AArch64 gas `.word` is FOUR bytes; on x86 gas it is TWO. An engine that knew a width for `.word` would silently halve or double every table on one of the two ports, which is precisely why `unitBytes` is dialect data. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-13 with the reference assembler rather than recalled — `aarch64-linux-gnu-as` on a file defining one label per directive, symbol offsets read back with `objdump -t`: `.byte`→1, `.hword`→2, `.short`→2, `.word`→4, `.long`→4, `.quad`→8, `.xword`→8. Consecutive offsets 0,1,3,5,9,13,21,29 — each delta IS the width of the directive above it.

★ THREE SPELLINGS, ONE VERB — gas takes `.zero`, `.space` and `.skip` for the same thing, and the FIRST operand is a byte COUNT rather than a value (`.byte 16` writes one byte 0x10; `.zero 16` writes sixteen 0x00). The OPTIONAL SECOND operand is the fill byte.
★★★ THE VERB WAS SPELLED `reserveZeroBytes` UNTIL 2026-08-13 AND THE RENAME IS THE CLOSE OF D-ASM-SPACE-DIRECTIVE-FILL-BYTE-UNMODELLED. The old name was TRUE while the fill was unmodelled and a second operand was refused; it stops being true the moment `.space 4, 7` writes `07 07 07 07`, and a config verb whose name states the wrong default is a lie the next reader inherits.
★★ AND `.zero` IS IN THE SAME ROW SET, WHICH IS MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED — the tempting reading is that `.zero` takes no fill and therefore needs its own verb. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-13 with `aarch64-linux-gnu-as` + `objdump -s`: `.space 4, 7` AND `.zero 4, 7` BOTH assemble rc=0 and BOTH emit `07070707`. One verb, an optional fill, three spellings.
⚠ TWO DELIBERATE DIVERGENCES FROM gas, both erring toward refusing rather than writing bytes nobody named: a fill outside one byte is REFUSED here (✔MEASURED, gas truncates `.space 4, 300` to `0x2c` with a warning and exits 0) — through the SAME `valueFitsUnit` chokepoint `.byte 300` already uses, so it is one module policy and not a second opinion; and a THIRD operand is refused outright. ⓘ A non-zero fill in a ZERO-FILL section (`.bss`) is NOT a divergence: gas exits 0 with `Warning: ignoring fill value in section '.bss'`, and this build warns and ignores it identically — the wire format stores no file bytes there, so there is nowhere for a pattern to live.

⚠ `.align` MEANS DIFFERENT THINGS ON DIFFERENT gas TARGETS — a byte count on some, a power of two on others (AArch64 reads it as a power of two, like `.p2align`). It is declared `ignoredAnnotation` because DSS derives function alignment from the format rather than from the source, so the ambiguity never has to be resolved; the day alignment becomes honoured, this row is the one that must grow a target-aware reading rather than a guess.

★★★ THE `.cfi_*` FAMILY — AND ON THIS PORT IT IS AN ADDITION, NOT A REPAIR. D-ASM-CFI-UNWIND-INFO-SILENTLY-DROPPED's own text records the asymmetry and warns about the wrong way to close it: the AT&T dialect carried all eighteen spellings as `ignoredAnnotation` (accepted and DROPPED — the defect), while THIS dialect carried ZERO, so `.cfi_startproc` in an aarch64 `.s` FAILED LOUD as an unknown directive — bar-compliant behaviour that simply could not read the input. Declaring them here as `ignoredAnnotation` 'for consistency with the sibling' would have propagated the defect into a second dialect in the name of tidiness. They arrive as REAL verbs or not at all.
★★ THE SPELLINGS AND THE MEANINGS ARE IDENTICAL TO THE AT&T PORT, AND THAT IS AN OBSERVATION RATHER THAN AN ASSUMPTION. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-17, `aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc 13.3.0 -O1 -S`: the compiler emits `.cfi_startproc`, `.cfi_def_cfa_offset`, `.cfi_offset 29, -16`, `.cfi_offset 30, -8`, `.cfi_remember_state`, `.cfi_restore 29`, `.cfi_restore_state`, `.cfi_endproc` — the same family, the same numeric operand form, no `#` sigil on the numbers. The two dialects differ on `.type`'s marker (`%function` vs `@function`), on `.word`'s width and on `.global` vs `.globl`; they do NOT differ here, and a row set that invented a difference would be describing the config file rather than gas.
⚠ THE OPERANDS ARE DWARF REGISTER NUMBERS AND THE COLUMN IS 30, NOT 16. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-17, `aarch64-linux-gnu-as` 2.42 + `readelf --debug-dump=frames`: the CIE prints `Return address column: 30` and `DW_CFA_def_cfa: r31 (sp) ofs 0` — x30 IS an ordinary register that also serves as the RA column, where x86_64's column 16 is synthetic and belongs to no register. That difference is the target's to state (`dwarfReturnAddressColumn` in `arm64.target.json`), never this document's.

⛔ `.cfi_signal_frame` — DECLARED AND REFUSED. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-17: it changes the CIE AUGMENTATION to 'zRS', which is a CIE-level property, and DSS emits one shared CIE per module. See the AT&T row for the full measurement.

⛔ `.cfi_escape` — DECLARED AND REFUSED, for the reason the AT&T row measures in full: it states RAW DWARF CFA BYTES nothing can validate or re-encode, and ✔MEASURED 2026-08-17 GNU as emits them verbatim with no length check, so a malformed escape silently EATS the following rules out of the unwind program at rc=0. Declared rather than left undeclared so the refusal names the construct and the next reader finds this note instead of 'adding the missing row'.
